sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) Netaji ____ promised independence to Indians saying, 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga'. (b) The watchwords of the ____ Revolution — liberty, equality and fraternity — inspired the whole world.

Fill in the blanks: The struggle for ____ was carried on by Subhas Chandra Bose from abroad. He found the outbreak of the ____ to be a convenient opportunity to strike a blow for the freedom of India.
Fill in the blanks: Netaji gave the famous battle cry '____'; the Indian flag was hoisted at ____ in March 1944.
Answer in one word each: (a) Which Act of 1919 allowed the British to imprison any person without trial? (b) Which British officer ordered firing at Jallianwala Bagh?

Match: (a) Lal-Bal-Pal (b) Swaraj Party (c) Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (d) Forward Bloc — (i) C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru (ii) Subhas Chandra Bose (iii) Radical nationalists (iv) Bhagat Singh and Chandrashekhar Azad
True or False: (a) The Simon Commission had no Indian member. (b) The Muslim League was founded at Lucknow in 1916.
questions.answer: (a) True (b) False — it was founded at Dacca in 1906 (the Lucknow Pact was in 1916).

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi launch the Non-Cooperation Movement in August 1920? Explain.
questions.answer: The Rowlatt Act allowed imprisonment without trial and the government ignored Indian protests; the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the injustice to the Khalifa (Khilafat issue) angered Indians. Gandhi felt no purpose was served by cooperating with such a government, so he asked people to withdraw cooperation non-violently.

or.q: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted by Indians? Give two reasons.
or.answer: (1) It had no Indian member — it was an all-white commission deciding India's constitutional future. (2) Indians saw it as an insult and a denial of their right to self-government, so they protested with black flags and 'Simon Go Back'.

questions.q: Why was the Khilafat Movement started?
questions.answer: During World War I Muslims supported the British on the understanding that the holy places of the Ottoman Empire would remain with the Khalifa. After the war the Ottoman Empire was divided and the Turkish Sultan (Khalifa) humiliated, so Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali started the Khilafat Movement.

questions.q: What do you understand by 'Purna Swaraj'?
questions.answer: Purna Swaraj means complete independence and sovereignty. The Congress adopted it as its goal at the Lahore session of 1929 and celebrated 26 January 1930 as Independence Day.

questions.q: Differentiate between the Moderates and the Radicals.
questions.answer: Moderates (1885–1905) had faith in British justice and placed demands through petitions within the law. Radicals (Lal-Bal-Pal) believed freedom was a right and used mass protests, boycott of foreign goods and swadeshi to involve the people.

questions.q: Why did Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt throw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly?
questions.answer: On 8 April 1929 they threw it to protest against the passage of the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Disputes Bill and to awaken the people, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad'; no one was hurt.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Examine the significance of 'Vande Mataram' in the nationalist movement of India.
questions.answer: Bankim Chandra Chatterji's hymn to the Motherland became the rallying cry of patriotic nationalists. It inspired generations to supreme self-sacrifice and expressed love for the motherland. It created such fear among the British that they banned the song.

or.q: How did regional organisations turn into a national organisation during colonial India?
or.answer: Many regional bodies such as the Indian Association, Bengal Presidency Association and Poona Sarvajanik Sabha raised voices against British rule separately. Leaders felt that joint work would make Indian demands stronger, which led to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1885 as an all-India body.

questions.q: Describe the main features of the Dandi March.
questions.answer: (1) Gandhi opposed the tax on salt, a basic need of everyone. (2) In March–April 1930 he marched from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi on the Gujarat coast. (3) On 6 April 1930 he broke the Salt Law by picking up sea salt. (4) It was peaceful, and farmers, traders and women joined in large numbers; Gandhi was arrested in May 1930. It began the Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.q: How did the First World War influence India? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Indian leaders supported Britain hoping for self-government after the war. (2) To repay war loans the British raised land revenue, increased prices, imposed income taxes and forcibly recruited soldiers, causing unrest. (3) Peasants and workers protested at Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. (4) The Lucknow Pact and Home Rule movement strengthened the demand for self-rule, and the division of the Ottoman Empire led to the Khilafat Movement.

questions.q: Who announced the Partition of Bengal? Describe its impact on Indian society.
questions.answer: Lord Curzon (1905). Impact: (1) Indians saw it as Divide and Rule and protested through meetings, processions and the press; Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis to show unity. (2) The Swadeshi and Boycott movements began; swadeshi mills, banks and stores were set up. (3) Students and women joined, the Radicals rose to prominence, and the partition was annulled in 1911.

questions.q: Describe Mahatma Gandhi's programme of the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920).
questions.answer: (1) Surrender of titles and honorary offices and resignation from nominated seats. (2) Boycott of government schools and colleges, courts, legislative councils and foreign goods. (3) Refusal to attend official functions or join the army for service in Mesopotamia. (4) Constructive programme: swadeshi, hand-spinning and weaving, removal of untouchability and Hindu–Muslim unity.

questions.q: Explain the role of revolutionaries and secret societies in the National Movement.
questions.answer: Angered by British repression, young revolutionaries formed secret societies in Punjab, Bengal, Maharashtra and UP. Khudiram Bose, Savarkar, Lala Hardayal (Ghadar Party), Bismil and Ashfaqullah (Kakori conspiracy), Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh (HSRA) attacked unpopular officials and British property. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged in 1931; their sacrifice made them symbols of national unity and inspired the people.

questions.q: Explain the formation of the Muslim League in India.
questions.answer: The British encouraged Muslims to form their own political body to weaken national unity. At the Muhammadan Educational Conference at Dacca, Nawab Salimullah Khan proposed it, and the All India Muslim League was founded on 30 December 1906 with the Aga Khan as President, to protect Muslim rights and represent them to the government. It is called the first fruit of Divide and Rule.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Why did Lord Curzon partition Bengal in 1905? How did Indians respond to it, and what does their reaction tell us about the spirit of nationalism at that time?
questions.answer: Why: Curzon said it was to improve administration, but the real aim was 'Divide and Rule' — to separate Hindus and Muslims and weaken the strong national movement in Bengal. Response: (1) widespread meetings, processions and press campaigns all over India; (2) Hindus and Muslims tied rakhis to each other; (3) the Swadeshi and Boycott movements — foreign goods were boycotted and swadeshi mills, banks and stores set up, with students and women taking part. Spirit: it showed that nationalism had become a mass feeling, that people were united across religions, self-reliant and no longer afraid of repression; the British had to annul the partition in 1911.

or.q: Why was the rise of radical nationalists considered a turning point in the freedom struggle? Explain their main beliefs and methods.
or.answer: Turning point: they ended the era of petitions and made the movement a mass struggle involving peasants, workers, students and women. Beliefs: (1) the British were exploiting India and draining its wealth; (2) freedom was a right, not a favour — 'Swaraj is my birthright'; (3) Indians must be self-reliant. Methods: (4) mass protests and criticism of government policy; (5) boycott of foreign goods and use of swadeshi; (6) national education and promotion of Indian industries. Leaders: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.

questions.q: Why was the Quit India Movement launched? Explain its main features.
questions.answer: Why: (1) the Cripps Mission (1942) failed to offer full independence; (2) wartime shortages and unemployment caused discontent; (3) leaders feared Japan would invade India because of the British presence. Features: (4) the Quit India resolution was passed at Bombay on 8 August 1942 with Gandhi's mantra 'Do or Die'; (5) all leaders were arrested on 9 August, so people led the movement themselves — burning government buildings and cutting railway and telegraph lines, with parallel governments in Ballia, Midnapore and Satara; (6) the British crushed it brutally, but it showed that independence was no longer a matter of bargain.

questions.q: Describe the role of Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army in the freedom struggle.
questions.answer: (1) Bose saw World War II as an opportunity to strike for freedom. (2) He escaped house arrest to Berlin in 1941, where Indians hailed him as 'Netaji' with 'Jai Hind'. (3) On Ras Bihari Bose's invitation he came to East Asia in 1943 and led the Indian Independence League and the INA (Azad Hind Fauj). (4) He gave the cries 'Chalo Dilli' and 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga'. (5) The INA hoisted the Indian flag at Kohima in 1944. (6) Though the INA collapsed, its patriotism inspired Indians and shook British confidence in the loyalty of Indian soldiers.
